faq.a: UV‑B penetrates epidermis, directly damaging DNA to form pyrimidine dimers; UV‑A causes indirect oxidative damage.
faq.q: Why is UV‑B more carcinogenic than UV‑A?

faq.a: Yes, regular use of broad‑spectrum SPF 30+ reduces UV‑B damage and lowers SCC risk.
Cryotherapy is suitable for AK but not for SCC; SCC requires surgical excision for cure.

exam: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 65‑year‑old farmer with a scaly, rough plaque on the forearm? — Actinic keratosis; explain UV‑B damage and premalignancy.
A patient presents with an ulcerated nodular lesion on the cheek. What is the next best step? — Excisional biopsy; discuss SCC staging and need for clear margins.
Why is 5‑fluorouracil preferred over cryotherapy for multiple AKs? — Discuss efficacy, patient comfort, and field‑effect treatment.
A 50‑year‑old HIV patient has a rapidly enlarging skin nodule. What red flag suggests metastatic disease? — Regional lymphadenopathy; explain immunosuppression increases SCC aggressiveness.
Explain why dermoscopy is useful but not definitive for SCC. — Describe vascular patterns, keratin plugs, and need for biopsy.

In a low‑resource setting, a patient has a suspicious lesion but no biopsy facility. What is the safest management? — Treat as SCC with wide excision and refer for histology if possible; emphasize sun protection.
Why should patients with AK be advised to avoid peak sun hours? — UV‑B intensity is highest 10–16 h; avoidance reduces DNA damage.
ai.title: Sunlight Exposure and Skin Cancer
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Sunlight, especially UV‑B, causes DNA pyrimidine dimers in keratinocytes. If repair fails, mutations accumulate, leading to actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma. Early detection and sun‑protection are key.

b: AK: rough, scaly papule; SCC: ulcerated or nodular lesion
sections.p: Sunlight exposure refers to contact with ultraviolet (UV) radiation, mainly UV‑B (280–315 nm). In pathology it is the inciting factor for actinic keratosis (AK) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Diagnosis is clinical, supported by dermoscopy and, if needed, biopsy.

b: T1: ≤2 cm, no ulcer; T2: >2 cm or ulcer; T3: >4 cm or deep invasion
sections.p: AK is a premalignant lesion; SCC is staged by TNM. In low‑resource settings, clinical staging (size, ulceration, depth) guides management.
Primary cause is cumulative UV‑B exposure. Modifiers include skin phototype, age, immunosuppression, and occupational outdoor work.

b: AK: erythematous, rough surface; SCC: ulcer, crust, bleeding
sections.p: Patients present with scaly plaques (AK) or ulcerated nodules (SCC). In advanced cases, pain, bleeding, or regional lymphadenopathy may occur.
Routine investigations are limited; dermoscopy and punch biopsy are gold standards. In resource‑poor settings, clinical assessment suffices.

t.b: Distinguishes AK from benign lesions by identifying keratin plugs and vascular patterns; a positive finding supports biopsy.
Confirms histology; shows keratinocyte atypia and invasion for SCC.
Rule out fungal infection if lesion is scaly; a negative KOH supports AK.

sections.p: Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, or regional lymphadenopathy suggest SCC or metastatic disease. Untreated SCC can invade bone or metastasise.

b: Cryotherapy: liquid nitrogen, 3–5 min per lesion
sections.p: Treat AK with cryotherapy, topical 5‑fluorouracil, or photodynamic therapy. SCC requires excision with clear margins; in low‑resource settings, wide local excision or Mohs if available. Adjunctive care includes sun‑protection and patient education.

t.b: Topical chemotherapeutic for AK; applied nightly for 4–6 weeks; monitors for erythema and peeling.
Indicated for SCC; ensures margin clearance; monitor for recurrence.

b: Sunscreen SPF 30+ applied 30 min before sun exposure
sections.p: Patients should be reviewed every 3–6 months for new lesions. Prevention focuses on broad‑spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, and avoiding peak sun hours.
Actinic keratosis can mimic seborrhoeic keratosis or psoriasis. SCC may resemble basal cell carcinoma or melanoma.
Dermoscopy may miss early SCC; biopsy may be non‑representative if sampling a non‑representative area. In HIV patients, atypical presentations occur.
